video_title: Bitcoin Survives Biggest Crypto Hack In History?!
gist: Pompliano and Jordi Visser discuss the roughly $6B Binance hack and its muted 5% Bitcoin reaction, AI/quantum security fears, the Anthropic S-1, Microsoft's 60,000-person buyout, rates and the November 4 refunding, and Visser's bullish Eli Lilly thesis. Visser is buying AI dips and sees a catalyst-driven recovery.

insights.claim: A roughly $6B Binance hack, rumored to involve North Korea, knocked Bitcoin only about 5%, which Pompliano reads as bullish since a comparable event a decade ago would have meant a 20-40% selloff.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Muted downside reaction suggests a maturing, less fragile market.

insights.claim: Visser argues Bitcoin's muted reaction reflects lower volatility relative to mega-caps, noting Google fell 13% and Intel 25% in the same stretch while Eli Lilly rose 10% in two days.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin's volatility is now below AI-linked equities, so do not expect the old 30-40% swings.

insights.claim: Visser says AI-driven hacking is a long-lasting reality, citing friends whose businesses had to be rebooted after attacks, and that hacks have been rising since roughly June.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cybersecurity risk is a structural, multi-year headwind and tail risk across crypto and corporates.

insights.claim: Stablecoin issuers such as Tether, Circle and World Liberty Financial froze multiple billions of the stolen funds, and Binance pledged to backstop user losses, so Binance would not need to cover the full $6B.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Issuer freezing power shows stablecoins are a policing chokepoint, trading off some bearer-asset ethos for trust.

insights.claim: Pompliano notes that the backstop and freezes erode the hardcore bearer-asset ethos, which could make regulated vehicles like ETFs more attractive.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Safety-net behavior may push flows toward institutional wrappers.

insights.claim: Visser views the hack as normal maturation like NASDAQ's electronic-trading glitches in 1999, and says banks now have skin in the game in tokenization and Bitcoin support, so security gets a plan.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bank involvement raises the security standard and makes shocks like this longer-term bullish.

themes.theme: Quantum and AI risk to Bitcoin

insights.claim: Visser heard secondhand that BlackRock is spending significant time on quantum risk, because quantum companies publicly claim they could break Bitcoin by 2028, though he thinks they are partly raising capital.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Quantum fear is the main concern he hears from investors and may force risk reduction until fixes are visible.

insights.claim: Visser says most worries he has heard in the last month about crypto are about quantum, and that incidents speed up the need for security work that the post-2022 recovery period neglected.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A credible post-quantum plan is a likely catalyst for the next leg up.

themes.theme: Bitcoin trading setup and bull case

insights.claim: Visser expects Bitcoin to retest its 200-day moving average, around 73-74K per Pompliano, after a rally from 59K to about 87-88K, and warns against assuming everything is fine post-hack.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect a test or brief break of the 200-day before any renewed uptrend.

insights.claim: Bitcoin has traded nearly one-for-one with semiconductors over the past month and a half, and an index of oil and 10-year rates has also correlated with it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Bitcoin is currently a macro and AI-beta trade, so hedge or size accordingly.

insights.claim: Visser describes 2026 as a horrible trading environment, with money made only in a small first-half window and mud since, and sees that continuing until a catalyst such as the November 4 quarterly refunding announcement.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Range-bound conditions favor patience and buying dips.

insights.claim: Visser's bull case for crypto is that nobody owns it, and a true bull market needs fundamentals led by tokenization, which he says gained a DTCC announcement this week, plus Stripe-seen agent commerce growth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Ownership is low among institutions and wealthy investors, leaving large upside if fundamentals show up.

insights.claim: Visser calls Bitcoin the purest AI trade and says AI will intensify downside from labor displacement and affordability pressures, pushing the system toward new monetary arrangements.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: He ties Bitcoin demand to AI-driven labor disruption rather than just liquidity.

themes.theme: Macro: rates, refunding and inflation base effects

insights.claim: Visser says AI capital raising has been concentrated in about five names, with over $1 trillion of equity and debt raised this year, and that this supply competed with Treasuries and contributed to higher rates and the market mud since September of last year.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Easing of debt issuance is a precondition for the AI trade to resume.

insights.claim: Oracle said at its investor day that it will not need to raise much money through 2030, after raising more than $60 billion since last September, which Visser calls the most important under-reported news of the week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Reduced AI financing overhang plus lower CDS stress is a positive for AI infrastructure names.

insights.claim: Visser says 10-year yields near 5% against about 2.5% breakevens mean roughly 250bp real yields, a major drag on crypto, gold, silver and AI stocks, but yields have fallen below the 50-day moving average this week.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A turn lower in real yields is the key swing factor for risk assets.

insights.claim: Visser flags speculation, including from Citi, that Treasury could cancel long-end supply at the November 4 refunding and shift issuance to the front end, which would not be yield curve control but would signal they do not want long yields higher.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: A shift away from long-end issuance would be a catalyst for duration and risk assets.

insights.claim: Visser expects disinflation next year as tariff effects roll off, Goldman forecasts roughly a 100bp drop in core PCE from base effects, DRAM prices have rolled over year over year, and oil is back near March levels.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Base effects should relieve inflation pressure and rate fears in the first half of next year.

insights.claim: Visser doubts 10-year yields fall to 3% soon because AI capital needs and heavy government debt keep issuance high, and he expects yield-curve-control-like intervention rather than traditional QE.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect a ceiling on long yields but no collapse; policy will be disguised.

insights.claim: Market breadth improved: the S&P 500 was about flat for the month, yet nine of 11 sectors were up and 350 of 500 names were up at least 2% versus only 70 down 2%, a 5:1 ratio.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Rotation away from mega-cap AI is broadening the market rather than signaling a bubble burst.

insights.claim: Triple-C rated companies now face about 16% borrowing costs, which Visser says requires very fast earnings growth against an S&P up only 10-11% year to date.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Stress in junk credit is a cautionary signal for weak balance sheets.

themes.theme: AI trade, bubble debate and labor versus capital

insights.claim: Visser made AI purchases three or four times in the last week and a half into panic, saying he is getting more positive and sees good entry points over the next six months even if the market stays muddy, and he is not worried about a bubble.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: He is buying dips in AI names into year-end.

insights.claim: Anthropic's S-1 was better than feared, with Visser saying it implies more than $100B of annualized revenue if October numbers after the latest model are included, and that the company serves 250 of the Fortune 500.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Clearing the S-1 overhang and the adoption data support AI demand ahead of an IPO.

insights.claim: Visser says hyperscalers as a group were flat for the year with Microsoft up 9%, and true SaaS names such as Salesforce have had a bad year, so bubble fears coexist with strong fundamentals.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Dispersion inside tech is large; AI beneficiaries and SaaS victims are diverging.

insights.claim: Microsoft offered buyouts to about 60,000 employees, 27% of roughly 223,000, versus 8,000 last time; at an assumed $400,000 all-in cost this is about $24B per year, which would bring headcount to 2020 levels while revenue is up about 70%.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Revenue per employee is surging, signaling AI-driven margin expansion.

insights.claim: Visser argues the Microsoft buyout creates a labor versus capital and tax arbitrage problem, since employees pay 50%+ in taxes while corporations pay less, making affordability a political issue that drives new policy and favors Bitcoin.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Expect political and fiscal responses to AI labor displacement.

insights.claim: Pompliano's public company cut compute costs from $550,000 per month in March 2026 by about 50%, hopes to move off frontier models to its own models for about 97% token cost savings, and with 10 people launched five products in five days.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: A concrete datapoint on AI productivity and deflationary cost pressure at small companies.

insights.claim: Pompliano says SpaceX is releasing roughly 50 to 100 new Grok bot features a week, and notes SpaceX revenue grew 160% year over year.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Shows extreme output velocity at AI-heavy firms.

insights.claim: Visser argues the bottleneck for building new data centers is memory, not GPUs, citing Intel's drop of 25% as PC sales suffer from higher memory costs and shortages.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Memory supply caps AI infrastructure growth and compresses multiples of constrained names.

insights.claim: Pompliano notes private AI valuations like Cognition and Ramp (40B+) and a rumored 30B raise for another firm are far richer than public valuations, with one founder claiming 10% daily growth, though Nvidia at about 12-13x earnings looks cheap.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Public AI multiples look more rational than private marks.

insights.claim: Visser says consumer AI adoption will be slow because of trust and hacking concerns, and he does not think individuals will pay, but young people who avoid AI will struggle to get jobs.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Monetization is enterprise-led, not consumer subscriptions.

insights.claim: Eli Lilly reported Q3 revenue of $24.4B up 39% versus $22.6B expected, volume up 53%, prices down 15%, gross margin 83%, and non-GAAP EPS of $7.48 against $6.26 expected, with Mounjaro at $10B and Zepbound at $5B.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Volume outpacing price cuts gives a very strong earnings beat and growth profile.

insights.claim: Eli Lilly raised 2026 revenue guidance to $91-92B from $85-87B, and Visser predicts it will become the world's largest company within five years, currently ranked ninth.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: He is overweight and calls Lilly his biggest position.

insights.claim: Visser says Lilly differs from Nvidia because its demand is non-cyclical and guaranteed by US healthcare spending, only about 10% of diagnosed US obesity patients are penetrated and under 3% globally, and orals will expand it.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Lilly offers growth without AI overbuild risk.

insights.claim: Visser believes Lilly uses its cash flow for AI bets such as TuneLab, an in-house data center, a Silicon Valley hub working with Nvidia, and buying unfinished biotech IP, giving call options in dementia, oncology and immunology.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Cash cow funding AI drug discovery creates optionality beyond GLP-1.

insights.claim: Visser says Palantir is the only software company he owns and is a growing position as it outperforms semis, but warns its high multiple could leave it flat for a year and a half like semiconductors.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Sovereign AI theme supports Palantir, but valuation risk limits upside timing.

themes.theme: AI use cases and Sylvia Legacy

insights.claim: Pompliano launched Sylvia Legacy, letting users nominate a person to receive their financial package and optional chat history if they fail to log in for about 60 days plus weekly warnings.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano
insights.so_what: Chat history is becoming an inheritable asset class; product-promotion context.

insights.claim: Visser says Meta's Muse model has the strongest memory for personal use such as tracking meals, and Pompliano used Grok bot for genealogy research and video editing into shorts.
insights.speaker: Jordi Visser
insights.so_what: Anecdotal evidence that agent memory and tooling drive consumer stickiness.
